author: Mia Brown
title: Public Meltdown: The Unseen Tension Between John F. Kennedy Jr. and Carolyn Bessette Before Their Wedding
text:
Screaming into each other’s faces from inches apart, John F.
Kennedy Jr. and Carolyn Bessette were not exactly looking their uber-glamorous best.
article image The scene in New York City’s Battery Park on February 1996 was a far cry from the idyllic island in Georgia where their society wedding was slated to take place seven months later.
Photographer Angie Coqueran, who captured the chaos unseen, later described the moment as one of profound discomfort.
The couple’s argument escalated to the point of physical confrontation, with Kennedy allegedly yanking Carolyn’s engagement ring so violently that it shattered in his hand. ‘The whole thing was very public, and it made me really uncomfortable and nervous,’ Coqueran told the Daily Mail last year. ‘Eventually they stopped arguing and there was a lot of sitting in silence on the park bench.’
When they finally left the park, Coqueran overheard Kennedy whispering to his fiancée: ‘I don’t even know her…
John F. Kennedy Jr. and Carolyn Bessette were in a heated argument in New York City’s Battery Park on February 1996. I don’t know what you’re talking about.’ This moment, now etched into the public imagination, hints at the turbulence that would define their relationship.
For a family known for its storied history of philandering and drama, the Kennedy name carried its own weight of expectation and scrutiny.
The official narrative, carefully curated by the Kennedy family, portrays the couple’s romance as a ‘glittering but doomed’ one, cut short by tragedy in July 1999 when Kennedy’s plane crashed into the Atlantic, killing him, Carolyn, and her sister Lauren.
The tragedy, which occurred when both John Jr. and Carolyn were in their thirties, preserved their memory as young, cool, and tragically beautiful.
Screaming into each other’s faces from inches apart, John F Kennedy Jr and Carolyn Bessette were not exactly looking their uber-glamorous best He was the founder of the hip magazine *George*; she was a senior publicist at Calvin Klein and a fashion icon.
Their doomed romance became a chapter in the so-called ‘curse of the Kennedy family,’ a narrative that The New York Times once mourned as ‘a family of unfinished journeys, of magnetic personalities cut down far too early.’
Now, Ryan Murphy, the controversial television writer and director behind *American Horror Story* and *American Crime Story*, is resurrecting their story in the latest installment of his *American Story* franchise: *American Love Story*.
The series will focus on the whirlwind courtship and marriage of John Jr. and Carolyn, with Sarah Pidgeon as Carolyn, Paul Kelly as John Jr., and Naomi Watts as his mother, Jacqueline.
Biographer Edward Klein described their relationship as ‘a doomed fairy tale, a nightmare of escalating domestic violence, suspicions of infidelity and drugs’ Murphy, known for his dramatic reinterpretations of real events, has faced criticism for taking liberties with history.
This raises questions about how he will portray the couple’s relationship, especially given the conflicting accounts in rival biographies.
Edward Klein’s 2003 book *The Kennedy Curse* paints a starkly different picture, depicting Carolyn as a ‘philandering and unhinged coke-head’ who arrived two hours late for her own wedding.
He described their relationship as ‘a doomed fairy tale, a nightmare of escalating domestic violence, suspicions of infidelity, and drugs – a union that seemed destined to end in one kind of disaster or another.’ These conflicting narratives underscore the complexity of the couple’s legacy, leaving audiences to wonder which version of their story Murphy will ultimately tell.
The public’s fascination with the Kennedys has never waned, and this new iteration of their story is sure to reignite debates about fame, tragedy, and the price of being part of a family that has long been both revered and reviled.
As the world watches *American Love Story*, the question remains: will it be a celebration of love, a cautionary tale, or something entirely different?
Carolyn Bessette-Kennedy’s life has long been a subject of fascination, controversy, and conflicting narratives.
In 2024, Elizabeth Beller’s biography *Once Upon A Time: The Captivating Life Of Carolyn Bessette-Kennedy* painted her as a tragically misunderstood figure—a woman of grace and resilience who was cruelly hounded by the media and the Kennedys’ shadowy legacy.
Beller’s portrayal, steeped in the ethos of the #MeToo era, framed Carolyn as a victim of systemic misogyny, a “perfect princess” who was forced into the role of a Stepford-esque political wife by a husband who wielded power like a weapon.
Yet, just as quickly, critics and other biographers have challenged this version, arguing that Carolyn’s story is far more complex, messy, and nuanced than Beller’s sentimentalized account suggests.
Edward Klein, the veteran journalist and biographer, offered a starkly different take in his analysis of the Kennedy-Bessette-Kennedy relationship.
He described it as a “doomed fairy tale, a nightmare of escalating domestic violence, suspicions of infidelity, and drugs.” Klein’s account, while not without its own controversies, painted a picture of a partnership fraught with tension, where power imbalances and personal demons collided.
John F.
Kennedy Jr., the scion of America’s most storied political family, was 31 when he met Carolyn, a woman who was 26 and hailed from a completely different world.
She was the daughter of an architectural engineer and a public school teacher, raised in the New York suburbs and later Greenwich, Connecticut.
Her journey from a modest background to the glittering heights of New York fashion was marked by intelligence, ambition, and a sharp wit that would later become a defining trait.
Carolyn’s path to Calvin Klein was as unconventional as it was meteoric.
After brief stints in modeling and nightclub promotion, she landed a sales job at Calvin Klein’s Boston store, a role that quickly elevated her due to her keen fashion sense and natural charisma.
By the time she moved to Manhattan, she was a rising star in the company, managing VIP clients with a blend of poise and precision.
It was here, in the heart of New York’s fashion scene, that she would cross paths with John F.
Kennedy Jr.—though the exact circumstances of their meeting remain maddeningly elusive.
Some say they met while jogging in Central Park; others claim it was at a party hosted by Calvin Klein’s second wife, Kelly Klein.
The most widely accepted theory, however, is that their relationship began when John Jr. visited the Calvin Klein showroom, where Carolyn was handling high-profile clients.
John F.
Kennedy Jr. was no stranger to the spotlight.
As the son of JFK Jr., he had been a national icon since childhood, winning the hearts of millions when he saluted his father’s flag-draped casket at the age of three.
His life was a tapestry of privilege and privilege’s pitfalls—he attended Brown University, dabbled in acting, law, and journalism, and co-founded the magazine *George*, which sought to blend politics with fashion and lifestyle.
His romantic history was equally colorful, with past relationships including Brooke Shields, Cindy Crawford, and Sarah Jessica Parker.
Yet, despite his fame and the trail of broken hearts he left behind, Carolyn was never cowed by celebrity.
In fact, it was her ability to navigate the world of high fashion and high society that made her an unlikely match for the Kennedy scion.
Maureen Callahan, in her book *Ask Not: The Kennedys And The Women They Destroyed*, painted a more critical portrait of Carolyn, one that diverged sharply from Beller’s romanticized version.
Callahan revealed that Carolyn struggled with substance abuse, using cocaine heavily to control her weight and antidepressants to cope with the relentless pressure of fame and marriage.
She also alleged that John Jr. was far from blameless, describing him as a man who “played fast and loose with Carolyn’s heart for years” before expecting her to conform to the role of a traditional housewife in their New York loft.
Callahan quoted a close friend of Carolyn’s, who claimed that John Jr. was determined to “groom” her for the role of John F.
Kennedy’s wife, a transformation that, in the friend’s words, “started to kill her.”
The tragedy of Carolyn’s story lies in the tension between these two extremes—the angelic, victimized princess and the flawed, self-destructive woman.
Some have suggested that the only people who truly understood the depths of their relationship were the two of them, both of whom died in the crash of a small Piper Saratoga plane on July 16, 1999.
Yet, even in death, the questions surrounding their lives remain unanswered.
Was Carolyn the victim of a patriarchal system that sought to mold her into a political wife?
Or was she a woman who, like so many others, struggled with the weight of fame, the pressures of marriage, and the expectations of a family that had long been in the public eye?
The truth, as always, seems to lie somewhere in between—a haunting, unresolved chapter in the Kennedy saga that continues to captivate and divide those who seek to understand it.
Carolyn’s legacy endures, not just as the wife of a Kennedy, but as a symbol of the complexities of fame, power, and personal identity.
Her story is a mirror held up to the American obsession with perfection, the media’s relentless hunger for scandal, and the ways in which even the most private lives can be dissected and reconstructed by the public.
Whether she was a victim, a villain, or something in between, Carolyn Bessette-Kennedy remains a figure of fascination—a woman whose life was as much a product of her own choices as it was of the forces that surrounded her.
In terms of personality and interests, they were not obviously compatible – she was a big party girl while his idea of a perfect weekend was a grueling hike in the mountains.
Their contrasting worlds seemed to collide in a way that defied logic, yet the magnetic pull between John F.
Kennedy Jr. and Carolyn Bessette-Kennedy was undeniable.
While John Jr. thrived in the quiet intensity of the outdoors, Carolyn reveled in the chaos of New York’s nightlife, her presence a whirlwind of laughter and glitter.
Their relationship, however, was far from a mere clash of lifestyles; it was a collision of two souls navigating the complexities of fame, family legacy, and personal identity.
Some have said that the only two people who really understood their relationship went down in that little Piper Saratoga plane, but the speculation seems set to continue.
The tragic plane crash in 1999, which claimed their lives along with their sister and her fiancé, left a void that even the most astute observers of their relationship could never fully fill.
Theories about their marriage, their secrets, and their unspoken struggles remain as elusive as the wind that carried them over the Atlantic that fateful day.
In terms of personality, they were not obviously compatible – she was a big party girl while his idea of a perfect weekend was a grueling hike in the mountains.
This divergence was not lost on those who knew them, but it was also a source of fascination.
John Jr., the scion of one of America’s most storied families, was a man shaped by the weight of history and the expectations of a dynasty.
Carolyn, on the other hand, was a woman who had built her own world from the ground up, a model and socialite who had never sought the spotlight until it found her.
Another reason why they didn’t immediately fall for each other was that they were both with other people when they met – John Jr was dating Hollywood actress Daryl Hannah while Carolyn was seeing Calvin Klein underwear model and future Baywatch star Michael Bergin. (The latter later claimed in a book published after her death that Carolyn’s sexual obsession with him continued after her marriage to John Jr.) The scandal of their meeting was as much a part of their story as the love that eventually grew between them.
Daryl Hannah, known for her role in *The Breakfast Club* and her activism, had a reputation for being fiercely independent, while Michael Bergin, a man who would later become a household name through *Baywatch*, was a figure of both glamour and controversy.
By 1994, however, John Jr and Carolyn were definitely dating and, predictably, the paparazzi couldn’t get enough of them.
The media’s continual presence in their lives meant, inevitably, that their public spats – which weren’t infrequent – were chronicled as fully as their glitzy party appearances.
John Jr, who had grown up in the glare of the world’s most invasive lens, seemed to relish the chaos, while Carolyn, who had once been a private woman, found herself thrust into a role she had never chosen.
He was used to – and some say, relished – relentless media attention but she’d never sought fame and found it difficult to handle, (Sarah Jessica Parker once observed that going out with John Jr taught her what it was really like to be famous) and complained to friends she couldn’t do anything to advance her career without being accused of exploiting the Kennedy name.
The weight of the Kennedy legacy was a double-edged sword, and for Carolyn, it was a burden she never asked for but could never escape.
In 1996, John Jr and Carolyn married in front of just 40 people in a tiny wooden church on an island off Georgia – albeit an event that involved a major security operation to ensure their privacy.
The ceremony was a stark contrast to the opulence of the Kennedys’ past, a quiet affirmation of their love in a world that had long since abandoned privacy.
Yet even in that moment of intimacy, the shadows of the media loomed large, their presence felt even in the most sacred of spaces.
As they moved into John Jr’s loft apartment in Manhattan’s Tribeca neighborhood, (besieged 24/7 by photographers and TV crews) the media chatter rapidly became fevered speculation over when she might have a baby, which Carolyn would fend off with jokes.
The world wanted a Kennedy heir, but Carolyn, who had always been a woman of her own making, seemed to resist the script that had been written for her.
Her laughter, though, was a defense mechanism, a way to deflect the pressure that was slowly closing in around her.
According to Klein, however, Carolyn’s refusal to give John Jr the children he craved – and indeed, her refusal to even have sex with him – was just one of the growing rifts between the couple.
The tension between them was not merely a matter of personal preference but a reflection of deeper, more insidious forces at play.
John Jr, who had always been a man of action, found himself increasingly frustrated by a wife who seemed to retreat into herself, her silence speaking louder than any words.
Although Klein credited Carolyn with a ‘shrewd, sharp, hard intelligence’, he said that she crumbled under the intense public attention, which not only increased her anxiety but also made her controlling. ‘It was clear to friends that Carolyn was cracking under the pressure,’ he wrote. ‘She displayed the classical signs of clinical depression.
A few months after the wedding, she began spending more and more time locked in her apartment, convulsed by crying gags…’ The weight of the world had finally caught up to her, and the cracks in her composure were beginning to show.
Carolyn’s downward spiral, Klein writes, had started before they married.
He recounted how, on her wedding day, she’d become ‘hysterical’ when she had trouble getting into her Narciso Rodriguez dress and ‘in a state of high anxiety’ was two hours late for the ceremony.
The dress, a symbol of elegance and perfection, had become a source of torment, a reminder of the expectations that had always been placed upon her.
The world had wanted a perfect Kennedy bride, and in that moment, Carolyn had failed to meet the standard.
After they wed, her behavior became ever more alarming, said Klein.
He reported how she stopped going out and became a ‘heavy user of street drugs,’ sitting in restaurants unaware she had ‘white rings around her nostrils.’ He said John Jr returned home one night to find her ‘sprawled on the floor in front of a sofa, disheveled and hollow-eyed, snorting cocaine with a gaggle of gay fashionistas –clothing designers, stylists, male models, and one or two publicists.’ The once-vibrant woman who had captured the world’s imagination was now a ghost of herself, lost in a haze of self-destruction and despair.
Carolyn Bessette-Kennedy and John F.
Kennedy Jr. were once the golden couple of the 1990s, their romance a blend of old money, Hollywood glamour, and the kind of magnetism that made headlines.
But behind the polished veneer of their public image lay a tempest of personal turmoil, a story that would later be dissected by biographers, journalists, and fans alike.
Klein, the biographer who first chronicled their relationship, painted a picture of a marriage unraveling under the weight of addiction, paranoia, and infidelity.
His account, drawn from secondhand anecdotes shared by John Jr. himself, described a partnership where ‘fiery tempers’ led to escalating violence.
One particularly harrowing moment came when John Jr. was rushed to the emergency room for surgery to repair a severed nerve in his right wrist—a consequence of a marital dispute that had spiraled out of control.
The cocaine that permeated their lives was a double-edged sword.
For Carolyn, it bred an almost pathological paranoia, especially when whispers of her husband’s rekindled romance with Daryl Hannah, the actress and environmental activist, reached her ears.
Klein claimed that these rumors triggered a cascade of anxiety, leading Carolyn to question the loyalty of her husband and the stability of their union.
Meanwhile, John Jr. was consumed by his own fears, convinced that Carolyn had returned to the arms of Michael Bergin, her ex-boyfriend and the man who had once been her fiancé.
According to Klein, the affair with Bergin didn’t end with Carolyn’s marriage to John Jr.—it persisted even after she moved into their shared loft, though the physical relationship eventually ceased after the wedding.
Klein’s account of their relationship is littered with anecdotes that paint a portrait of a woman who was both magnetic and volatile.
One particularly salacious detail came from Bergin’s former manager, who reportedly told Klein that Carolyn had once been found hiding under the model’s staircase, a moment that hinted at the depths of her desperation or perhaps her desire to provoke.
On another occasion, she allegedly broke a window to gain entry to Bergin’s apartment, climbing up his fire escape in a display of reckless behavior that seemed to defy the decorum expected of someone in Carolyn’s position.
These stories, while shocking, were part of a larger narrative of a marriage that was both public and private, a union that was constantly being scrutinized by the media and the public.
By 1997, the cracks in their relationship had become too wide to ignore.
John Jr. eventually moved out of their loft and into a hotel, a decision that some close to him believed was an attempt to reconcile the fractures in their marriage.
However, the couple’s final days were marked by a series of public spats that were as much a product of their personal struggles as they were of the relentless media attention that followed them.
The press, ever hungry for a glimpse into the lives of the famous, chronicled every argument, every party, and every moment of discord as if they were the only story worth telling.
This constant exposure turned their private battles into public spectacles, a reality that neither Carolyn nor John Jr. seemed to escape.
In 2024, Elizabeth Beller attempted to reframe the narrative of Carolyn’s life, writing a biography that sought to rehabilitate her image in the wake of the controversies that had surrounded her.
Beller’s work, however, was met with skepticism by the Washington Post, which described it as ‘dewy-eyed’ and overly sympathetic to Carolyn’s plight.
While Beller dismissed Klein’s more salacious claims, her own book barely addressed the drug allegations that had been central to the couple’s downfall.
Instead, she focused on a sanitized version of Carolyn’s life, quoting a friend who claimed she ‘barely drank wine’ and downplaying the alleged affairs that had been so central to the couple’s marital strife.
Beller’s portrayal of Carolyn was one of warmth and kindness, a woman who, according to her biographer, was ‘warm, funny, effervescent, and an extremely good friend.’ She even highlighted moments of compassion, such as Carolyn’s insistence that John Jr. reach out to Prince William and Harry after the death of their mother, Diana.
Beller argued that the press had painted Carolyn as ‘manipulative, crazy, cold [and] icy,’ a characterization she believed was entirely false. ‘She was someone who practiced random acts of kindness on a regular basis,’ Beller told Women’s Wear Daily, a sentiment that seemed to contradict the darker aspects of Carolyn’s life that had been so thoroughly documented by Klein and others.
Yet even Beller could not entirely ignore the reality of the couple’s troubled marriage.
She acknowledged that Carolyn had been prescribed antidepressants by the early 1990s, a sign of the psychological toll that their relationship had taken.
The marriage, she conceded, was in turmoil by 1999, with the couple seeking counseling as a last-ditch effort to salvage their union.
One particularly poignant moment, as recounted by Beller, was a break-up dinner where John Jr. handed Carolyn a letter from a close friend who accused her of being ‘a user, a partier, that she was out for fame and fortune.’ The letter, which described Carolyn as someone who ‘dated guys around town,’ was tossed at her by John Jr. before he left the room, a moment that Beller described as the final rupture in a relationship that had already been frayed beyond repair.
As for the media’s role in all of this, it is hard to imagine that Ryan Murphy, the showrunner known for his dramatizations of real-life tragedies, would pass up the opportunity to bring this story to the screen.
The couple’s final days, marked by public infidelity, addiction, and the looming shadow of their own deaths, offer a narrative that is as tragic as it is compelling.
Whether the public will be able to reconcile the conflicting accounts of Carolyn’s life—whether she was a victim of circumstance or a woman who chose to play the role of the troubled heiress—remains to be seen.
What is certain, however, is that the story of John F.
Kennedy Jr. and Carolyn Bessette-Kennedy will continue to be told, in books, in documentaries, and perhaps even in the next great American tragedy that the entertainment industry so loves to mine for drama.
